claims.text: The FeNiCrMn alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi by removing Co.
The initial FeNiCrMn material is a homogenized, water-quenched, single-phase FCC bulk single crystal.
Removing Co alters local lattice distortion in FeNiCrMn.
Removing Co modifies solute-atmosphere formation and reduces dynamic solute pinning.
The altered lattice distortion and solute atmosphere change the dislocation glide-resistance landscape.
At low temperatures, reduced phonon damping enhances dislocation inertia.
Enhanced dislocation inertia helps dislocations overcome obstacles strengthened by local lattice distortions.
The proposed low-temperature mechanism produces a sharper increase in CRSS upon cooling.
At high temperatures, the absence of Co diminishes robust solute-atmosphere formation.
Robust solute atmospheres cause Cottrell-type pinning and serrated flow in Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi.
Reduced high-temperature solute pinning in FeNiCrMn produces a smaller CRSS increment and smoother flow than in CoCrFeMnNi.
The dual low- and high-temperature mechanism preserves a favorable strength–ductility balance.
FeNiCrMn will have room-temperature CRSS similar to that of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi under matched testing conditions.
FeNiCrMn will exhibit a steeper CRSS increase upon cooling than CoCrFeMnNi.
FeNiCrMn will exhibit reduced or delayed high-temperature serrated flow relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
The predictions apply to single-phase FCC bulk single crystals in compression from approximately 10 K to 1373 K and at strain rates from 1×10^-4 to 1×10^-2 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The conditions exclude temperatures below the inertial regime, while the intervention and boundary extend to cryogenic temperatures near 10 K and the mechanism specifically relies on low-temperature inertial effects.

The conditions exclude temperatures above the onset of diffusion-controlled mechanisms, but the proposed range extends to about 1373 K and the high-temperature explanation invokes diffusion-associated solute-atmosphere formation and pinning.

The low-temperature account says enhanced inertia allows dislocations to overcome obstacles, yet directly associates this easier obstacle traversal with a sharper increase in CRSS; the competing effects are not reconciled.
